title: Why association alone does not identify causation
learning_objectives: Distinguish an observed association from a causal effect.
Identify confounding and reverse causation as alternative explanations.
Recognize how random assignment helps identify causal effects.

sources.title: Analyzing Findings: Correlation Does Not Indicate Causation

misconceptions.description: A strong or statistically significant correlation proves that one variable caused the other.
Controlling for one measured variable removes every possible confounder.

critical_errors.description: States that association alone establishes causal direction.
Claims that observational adjustment guarantees removal of all confounding.

teaching_brief.goal: Help the learner generate and test alternative explanations for an observed association.
teaching_brief.learner_profile: An undergraduate who tends to read causal language into correlational findings.
instructions: Use one example with a plausible confounder and one with reverse causation.
Ask what intervention and comparison would identify the causal question.
Distinguish random sampling from random assignment.
Have the learner rewrite an overclaimed headline.
prohibited_disclosures: Do not reveal held-out item wording.
Do not say that statistical significance alone proves causality.

pretest.prompt: People carrying lighters have higher rates of lung disease. Why does this not show that lighters cause the disease?

choices.text: Smoking can cause both lighter carrying and lung disease.
Lung disease always causes lighter purchases.
The sample must contain no people.

pretest.prompt: What is the main causal advantage of random assignment in a sufficiently large experiment?

choices.text: It tends to balance both observed and unobserved pre-treatment causes across groups.
It guarantees every measurement is error-free.
It replaces the need for a comparison group.

posttest.prompt: Students who attend optional tutorials earn higher grades. Which is a plausible confounder?

choices.text: Prior motivation may increase both attendance and grades.
Tutorials and grades are the same variable.

posttest.prompt: A survey finds poor sleep associated with anxiety. What alternative direction must be considered?

transfer.prompt: Neighborhoods with more trees have lower summer temperatures. Which study most directly tests whether adding trees lowers temperature?

choices.text: Randomly assign comparable sites to receive trees or not, then measure temperature under a declared protocol.
Repeat the same correlation in the same data.
Ask residents whether trees feel causal.

transfer.prompt: A headline says 'Reading news causes political participation' from an observational correlation. What is the most accurate revision?

choices.text: News reading was associated with participation; causal direction and confounding remain unresolved.
The correlation proves reading is the only cause.
Observational data can never contain useful information.
